proposals.subject: Bathysaurus deep-sea lizardfish
proposals.title: Above the waiting place
proposals.content:
I followed something off the bottom. It went up. I followed again.

Then it was gone, and I was still going. My fins were spread and there was nothing against my belly. I had spent so long waiting for things to come within reach that I had forgotten how much water I could reach myself.

On the way down I found my old hollow. There was something moving in it.

I passed over very quietly.
proposals.review: Source explicitly identifies swimming Bathysaurus cf. mollis in the Mariana region. Pale body and golden eye fit Severin. The pursuit, hollow and decision to pass are fiction, not a documented sequence. Swimming changes his relationship to waiting; no teeth-apology joke or audience. Lead should judge whether the final restraint repeats his earlier shrimp restraint; this draft makes the abandoned hunting position the object of attachment.

media.sourceCaption: Deep-sea lizardfish (Bathysaurus cf. mollis) typically lurk on the seafloor, hiding in wait for unsuspecting prey…but this one surprised us as it swam up and through the water column as we explored an extinct hydrothermal vent chimney in the Mariana region.
media.attribution: NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2016 Deepwater Exploration of the Marianas

proposals.subject: Limulus polyphemus
proposals.title: Finding the rim
proposals.content:
There were shells on her shell. I tried to hold her and caught one of those instead.

She kept moving. I let go, scrambled after her, and found the edge underneath. This time I could feel her moving through my grip.

Then she began to dig. Sand came back against my face. I shifted a little, expecting to be shaken off.

She dug deeper. I held on.
proposals.review: Requires explicit adult male canon detail: Hugo is the smaller upper-right attached animal, not the foreground female. NPS identifies male clasping female during spawning. Clasping and spawning are source-grounded; failed first grip, pursuit and uncertainty are fictional. Attached mollusk shells are visible but not assigned a species. New intimacy and bodily contact, rather than another joke about his own passengers.

proposals.subject: Muusoctopus sp.
proposals.title: Before I opened out
proposals.content:
The brittle stars were moving all round the stone. I thought I had disturbed them, so I stopped.

They kept going. The light behind me was getting stronger.

I had been deciding whether to spread myself out and look difficult to swallow. By the time I finished deciding, the little bodies were nearly out of reach.

I followed with my arms close.
proposals.review: Unpublished alternative to the held aquatic26 reaching-friend draft, not approval. Source reports octopus apparently unbothered while brittle stars move; escape and changed fear strategy are fictional. Too close to her existing first fear/display event, and brittle-star detail is weak at feed width. Do not count this as ready.

media.sourceCaption:
At a depth of 1,650 meters (5,414 feet), during the seventh dive of the 2023 Shakedown + EXPRESS West Coast Exploration expedition, we came upon this deep-sea octopus in the genus Muusoctopus. It didn’t seem too bothered or impressed by the presence of remotely operated vehicle Deep Discoverer, but if you look closely at the seafloor around it, you’ll notice several brittle stars who had other ideas and are on the move!
Learn more

proposals.subject: Parapagurus sp. with Epizoanthus colony
proposals.title: A little to the left
proposals.content:
I said it was safe because I could see all the way across.

The first black stone shifted under a leg. I put another leg down. That stone shifted too.

She said we were tilting. I said I knew.

After we had gone a little farther, I asked her to tell me sooner.

She did. I moved the leg she suggested. For several steps I managed not to explain why I had already been about to do that.
proposals.review: Crab genus, orange legs and hairy white claws fit Quentin, and source describes a movable nodule field. Existing guest is only called an anemone; new source explicitly identifies Epizoanthus coral/zoantharian. Cannot silently identify that colony as the same singular passenger. Hold until a deliberate scientifically coherent canon decision. Speech, rolling individual stones and cooperation are fiction.

sourceReview.sourceCaption:
This deep-sea lizardfish (Bathysaurus mollis) was seen on Dive 08 of the Mountains in the Deep: Exploring the Central Pacific Basin expedition. Bathysaurus have beautiful, yellow eyes and a mouth full of impressive teeth. They are apex predators in the abyss and are known to strike at other large fishes. These lizardfish are widely observed on abyssal plains. Scientists were able to identify this one down to species (Bathysaurus mollis) due to its pale coloration.
From: A Dive Into the Abyss.
sourceReview.attribution: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Mountains in the Deep: Exploring the Central Pacific Basin
sourceReview.visibleScene: Pale lizardfish head on sediment. Exact SHA already bound to Severin, The softer face.

sourceReview.sourceCaption: This glass sponge of the genus Caulophacus was seen while exploring on a ridge extending to the southeast of Castellano Seamount, south of the Midway Islands, as part of the 2016 Hohonu Moana: Exploring Deep Waters off Hawaiʻi expedition. These sponges, which belong to the Class Hexactinellida, get their common name of “glass sponge” because their skeletons are made of silica, which is the same material used to make glass…but glass sponges are not glass, per se.

sourceReview.sourceCaption:
This chrysogorgid octocoral, with its characteristic spiral form, belongs to the genus Iridogorgia. This stunning example was seen in the northwestern Gulf of Mexico during a 2012 expedition. Note the squat lobsters delicately perched atop its branches. Characteristics that can help scientists identify the type of Iridogorgia include the distance between parts of the coil along the main axis and the shape of the polyps.
This image won the Explorer’s Choice Photo Contest for the ‘Exploring the Seafloor’ category as part of our Celebrating Our Ocean Planet campaign.
From: Explorer’s Choice Photo Contest Archive.
sourceReview.attribution: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Gulf of Mexico 2012

sourceReview.sourceCaption:
NOAA Ocean Exploration, Seascape Alaska.  
Here’s a mesmerizingly close look at an octopus (Muusoctopus sp.) to celebrate #OctopusFriday.
This amazing imagery was captured on remotely operated vehicle Deep Discoverer‘s cameras during a Seascape Alaska 5 dive to explore at 3,180 meters (2 miles) depth on a seamount in the Gulf of Alaska. While super cool to look at, these close zooms also provide scientists important details (like the two rows of suckers on the animal’s arms) that help in identification and yield new insights.

A deepwater hermit crab (family Parapaguridae) makes its way across soft sediment on the southern flank of Blake Ridge, off the coast of Georgia during the Windows to the Deep 2018: Exploration of the Southeast U.S. Continental Margin expedition. sourceReview.sourceCaption:
The armored searobin, Scalicus engyceros, was one of the fishes that famous ichthyologist David Starr Jordan, the original president of Stanford University, reported among the specimens floating offshore of a 1919 lava flow from Mauna Loa. This individual was seen during a dive on August 29, 2015, off Keahole Point, several miles north of the 1919 lava flow on the Kona Coast of Hawaii Island.
From: Volcano Fish.
sourceReview.attribution: NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2015 Hohonu Moana
sourceReview.visibleScene: Orange Scalicus engyceros with short rostral prongs and large dark white-edged fins swimming above mud. Exact species source cannot automatically establish Rue or Giles; Giles swimming lesson spent.

sourceReview.sourceTitle: The Armored Searobin and the Brittle Star
sourceReview.sourceCaption:
During the Océano Profundo 2015: Exploring Puerto Rico’s Seamounts, Trenches, and Troughs expedition, while exploring the top of a Late Oligocene to Pilocene platform carbonate sequence and traversed a relatively minor fault scarp. This fault is the easterly extension of an approximately 100-kilometer-long fault system that forms the northern wall of the rift between the Dominican Republic and Puerto Rico, when witnessed an unusual encounter.
Seeing two deep-sea animals interacting with each other is rare. What is particularly rare is when they behave the opposite of how we expect them to. As we approached this armored searobin, a brittle star climbed on top of it. We watched to see if the fish would try to eat the brittle star, but as it turns out, it just wanted to dislodge the extra baggage. The brittle star then proceeded to climb on top of the sea robin two more times…persistent little guy!
sourceReview.attribution: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Exploring Puerto Rico’s Seamounts, Trenches, and Troughs
sourceReview.visibleScene: Red armored searobin with very long paired rostral prongs beside pink brittle star. Source explicitly describes repeated climbing. Atlantic fish does not establish continuity with existing Pacific searobins.
